author: Shakespeare
title: Falstaff’s prose, the King’s verse
where: *Henry IV, Part 2*: Act 1, Scene 2; Act 3, Scene 1; Act 5, Scene 5
about: Sir John Falstaff, a fat old knight, has been the companion of Prince Hal (Henry of Monmouth), heir to the throne. In the first passage, in prose, the Lord Chief Justice, who once jailed the Prince, stops Falstaff in a London street. In the second, in verse, the sick King, Henry IV, who took the crown from Richard II, is awake at one in the morning. In the third the old King is dead, and the Prince, just crowned Henry V, passes Falstaff, who waits near Westminster Abbey.

view.says: Auden wrote that Falstaff, who belongs to a comic world of play, cannot live in the world of political history, where Shakespeare sets him. Its matter is earthly justice: the old King pays for deposing a lawful king, and his son, rejecting Falstaff in public, shows his subjects a just ruler. By *Charity* Auden means love: he calls Falstaff’s tireless effort to make people laugh a comic picture of a love that keeps nothing back.
view.quote: a comic symbol for the supernatural order of Charity as contrasted with the temporal order of Justice symbolized by Henry of Monmouth
view.source: “The Prince’s Dog,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 183–84, 186–90, 198, 203–06; “Brothers & Others,” in the same book, p. 221

lenses.label: Cross
lenses.name: chiasmus
lenses.plain: a crossing: two things are named, then named again in the opposite order
lenses.why: Falstaff twice answers the Chief Justice with the judge’s own words crossed, which makes a wish of one charge and turns the other on the Prince; Auden said he uses word-play on purpose, to be liked and treated kindly.
lenses.caption: The Chief Justice makes three charges, and twice Falstaff answers in the judge’s own words, crossed. Slender means and a waste that is great come back as means greater and a waist slenderer. You have misled the Prince comes back as the Prince hath misled me. Rhetoric calls this chiasmus. It makes the second charge a wish and turns the third on the Prince. In Act 2 the Justice says he knows Falstaff’s way of twisting the true cause the false way. According to a student’s notes, Auden said in class in 1941 that Falstaff goes back to childish things, word-play among them, on purpose, to be liked and treated kindly.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. Chiasmus as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it, and its entry for *antimetabole*, the same words repeated in reverse order. The Chief Justice’s words in [Act 2, Scene 1](#/read/henry-iv-2/a2s1:71). What Auden told his class: Donald Pearce’s notes of the lecture, p. 147.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: The meaning given here is the lexicon’s third sense of *great*. Its first sense is large in size, and there it quotes the *great belly* of the last reply.
The Quarto of 1600 prints *waste* in both speeches, and *slender*, not *slenderer*, in the reply; the Folio of 1623 has *wast* here and *waste* there.
Outside this exchange the play has the word once, as a noun. In Act 5 the new King banishes Falstaff as he has banished the rest of those he calls his *misleaders*.

lenses.why: The replies take the judge’s great, slender and waste as words of size, so each charge about how Falstaff lives is answered with his body; Auden wrote that Falstaff cannot be conceived as anything but old and fat.
lenses.caption: The Justice’s words are about how Falstaff lives: great infamy, slender means, great waste. Falstaff takes each as a word of size: a man in his belt cannot live in less, he wishes his waist slenderer, his belly is great. The lexicon of Shakespeare’s words files the judge’s slender under insufficient and Falstaff’s under thin, and marks the pun on waste and waist, which the 1600 printing spells alike. Later in the scene Falstaff says he was born with a round belly. Auden wrote that Falstaff cannot be conceived as anything but old and fat, and that this claim of his is believed.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Alexander Schmidt’s *Shakespeare-Lexicon* under Great, Infamy, Slender, Waste, Waist and Mislead; its entries for *slender*, *waste* and *waist* cite these lines. The Quarto of 1600, in the Internet Shakespeare Editions transcription, and Falstaff’s [later answer](#/read/henry-iv-2/a1s2:120) about his birth. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 183–84.

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.why: The charges make Falstaff the doer, and in his replies I only wishes and is; Auden wrote that he speaks only to show himself, and that his self-description is not complete without this last reply.
lenses.caption: In the charges Falstaff is the one who does things: you live, you have misled, and the means and waste are his. In the replies he is not. The one who lives is any man in his belt, and the one who misleads is the young prince. His I takes two verbs only: I would, a wish, twice, and I am. In his essay “The Prince’s Dog” Auden wrote that Falstaff speaks for one reason only, to show himself, and that almost all he says restates one theme, I am that I am. Near the end of the essay he says this does not describe him completely: Falstaff must also add the last reply here.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 186 and 207.

lenses.label: Play
lenses.what: which parts of the play are in verse and which in prose, and who speaks which

speakers.speaker: the Prince, before he is king
the Prince as King Henry V

lenses.why: Falstaff speaks in none of the nine scenes without prose, and the Prince speaks no prose after the scene where he bids Falstaff good night; Auden wrote that Falstaff belongs to comic opera and cannot exist in the chronicle.
lenses.caption: This exchange is prose, like nearly all that Falstaff says: 5,373 words of prose in the play and eleven lines set as verse. Nine of its nineteen scenes have no prose, and he speaks in none of them. The old King speaks only verse. The Prince speaks prose in Act 2, changes to verse when Peto comes in with news from the north, and never speaks prose again. Shakespeare used prose for comic scenes, and moved between prose and verse as subject or tone required. Auden wrote that Falstaff belongs by nature to comic opera, and that Shakespeare puts him into a political chronicle where he cannot exist.
lenses.stands: A count made on the text printed here: every line it sets as verse and every word of every speech it sets as prose, scene by scene and speaker by speaker. The Prince’s change to verse at [Peto’s entrance](#/read/henry-iv-2/a2s4:291). E. A. Abbott’s *Shakespearian Grammar*, section 515a, and Paull F. Baum’s *Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4, on prose and verse. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 221.

plates.heading: The King alone: lines 1 to 5 and 23 to 28 of his speech

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: ten syllables and five beats, the line beginning off the beat

points.say: At this stop the sentence about his subjects ends.
The voice gives the middle beat of this half-line no stress. Said quickly, the half-line can be heard with two stresses, not three.
At this stop the last question to Sleep ends.

lenses.why: The speech’s only two twelve-syllable lines are the two where the King turns to a new hearer, each made of two six-syllable halves that meet where a sentence ends.
lenses.caption: The King’s speech is in lines of ten syllables and five beats, the line beginning off the beat. Two of its twenty-eight lines have twelve syllables, six beats by the same count, and both are shown: the second line and the last but one. Each stops in the middle, where a sentence ends, six syllables on either side. At the first stop the King turns to Sleep, at the second from Sleep to the low. A six-beat line tends to split into three and three, and in Shakespeare it is often two short verses joined. The line is lengthened at the King’s two turns to a new hearer, and nowhere else in the speech.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and a count of syllables in all twenty-eight lines of [the speech](#/read/henry-iv-2/a3s1:5) as printed here. Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4, on the six-beat line. E. A. Abbott, *A Shakespearian Grammar*, sections 493 and 500. The Quarto of 1600 and the Folio of 1623, which print each long line as one line.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.why: The closing rhyme makes one unit of an order to the low and a statement about the crowned head, with one verb for both; Auden gave its last line as the father’s word on how uneasy a king is.
lenses.caption: The speech ends on a rhyme: lie down, a crown. A rhyme returning at once makes its two lines one unit. Within it the last question to Sleep ends at mid-line, and an order to the low and a statement follow. One verb serves both: the low lie down, the crowned head lies uneasy. Lecturing in New York in 1946 and 1947, Auden said that father and son each speak of how uneasy a king is: the father in this speech, whose last line he quotes, the son in Henry V. In Act 5 of this play the son, newly king, says that majesty sits not so easy on me.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4, on the short couplet. Auden: *Lectures on Shakespeare* (2000), p. 107, a text made from students’ notes. The new King’s words in [Act 5, Scene 2](#/read/henry-iv-2/a5s2:49).

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.why: After one question about himself the King drops I and my and ends on a King, the head, a crown; Auden called his rhetoric hollow and said he has come to feel something is wrong with him.
lenses.caption: The King says I or my four times in the first five lines, and not once in the twenty-three that follow. His first question is about himself, how have I frighted thee, and he does not come back to it. His last question holds its second verb, Deny, back two lines and ends on a King, the place of most weight; the last line has the head and a crown. Auden told his class in 1941 to notice how hollow this King’s rhetoric is throughout the play. He traced it to a life of not listening to his feelings, which leaves the King feeling that something is wrong with him.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and a search of [the whole speech](#/read/henry-iv-2/a3s1:5) as printed here for *I*, *me*, *my*, *mine*, *we* and *our*. William Strunk, *The Elements of Style* (1918), rule 18, on the end of a sentence. What Auden told his class: Donald Pearce’s notes of the lecture, pp. 147–48.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: The Quarto of 1600 prints *season* here. The Folio of 1623 prints *Sea-Boy*, and the text given here follows it.
A few lines after the speech the King calls his kingdom a body in which rank diseases grow.
The lexicon sets this line among the uses of the word for medicines. They stand under its wider sense: whatever is used to gain an end.
The lexicon cites the word twice from this speech. In its seventh line, not shown here, the pallets in the smoky cribs are *uneasy*, and Sleep lies stretched on them.

lenses.why: The King calls Sleep partial, a giver to one and a denier to another; Auden wrote that this King did an injustice in taking the crown, and that impartial justice is his son’s duty as king.
lenses.caption: The King calls Sleep partial, inclined to favor one party over the other, and asks whether it can give its rest to a ship’s boy and deny it to a king. The lexicon of Shakespeare’s words files this deny under refusing to grant, the sense in which a suit is granted or denied. Auden wrote that this King, in taking the crown, did an injustice that he and his kingdom must pay for, and that impartial justice is what his son, once king, has a duty to keep. The play has partial nowhere else, and has impartial twice, in Act 5, both times said of the Chief Justice.
lenses.stands: Alexander Schmidt’s *Shakespeare-Lexicon* under Partial and Deny, which cite these lines, and under each of the other words explained. The lines themselves. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 188 and 190. A search of the text printed here for *partial* and *impartial*; the second stands in [the Chief Justice’s](#/read/henry-iv-2/a5s2:42) and [the new King’s](#/read/henry-iv-2/a5s2:61) speeches in Act 5, Scene 2.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: ten syllables and five beats, the line beginning off the beat, without rhyme

points.say: A stress where the measure has no beat, directly after the stop. The period is an editor’s: the Folio of 1623 has a colon here and the Quarto of 1600 a comma.
Counted here as one syllable. It can also be heard as two, with an eleventh syllable past the last beat.

lenses.why: Falstaff’s part is prose, and his call to the King is a full verse line that three stops make halting.
lenses.caption: All three speak verse. Falstaff’s part is prose: only eleven of his lines are set as verse, three of them his calls to the King in this scene. The third, shown here, fills the measure, ten words of one syllable, every second one stressed, and three stops break it in four; a line with several pauses moves haltingly. The King’s answer stops after six syllables, and his first order, Fall, takes a stress after the stop. Falstaff’s next speech is prose.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and a count of Falstaff’s verse and prose in the text printed here. Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 5, on the pause, and E. A. Abbott, *A Shakespearian Grammar*, section 453, on the stress after a pause. Falstaff’s [next speech](#/read/henry-iv-2/a5s5:60), and the Quarto of 1600 and the Folio of 1623 for the stops.

lenses.label: Names
lenses.why: Falstaff claims the King as his own three times in one line; the King gives him no name, three labels and five orders; Auden said Falstaff has only personal ties and the Prince none, so they had to break.
lenses.caption: Falstaff’s line names the King three times, each time as his own: My King, My Jove, my heart. The King gives him no name, here or in the seventeen lines to come. He calls him that vain man, old man, a fool and jester. Auden told his class in 1941 that Falstaff can form only personal ties and the Prince none, so their break had to come; later he wrote that to the Prince he matters no more than a court jester would. The King gives him five orders here. The last, Reply not, forbids the sort of answer shown in the first passage, and Falstaff makes none.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the rest of [the King’s speech](#/read/henry-iv-2/a5s5:57). What Auden told his class: Donald Pearce’s notes of the lecture, p. 147. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 191. Falstaff’s replies in the first passage, and his [next words](#/read/henry-iv-2/a5s5:60), which are to Shallow.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: In Act 1 the Archbishop says the country’s greedy love has *surfeited*. Auden quotes that line where he writes that the sight of Falstaff’s paunch is a reminder that England is not healthy.
The Prince used the verb of himself in Act 2, when he blamed himself for profaning the time and said good night to Falstaff. Auden wrote that their friendship ends with that good night.
Falstaff has said the word twice in this scene, for a favor he means the King to do and as the King’s title. In Act 2 he set the Prince’s *grace* against his flesh in a joke.
The lexicon leaves two senses open: foolish from birth, or put up with only by fools. The Quarto and the Folio both spell the word with *borne*.

lenses.why: The King’s words are of age and the grave; Auden wrote that Falstaff’s world of play has no time, that in Henry IV he is drawn into history, where people die, and that music let him feel time stop.
lenses.caption: Four of the King’s phrases speak of age and death: old man, white hairs, so old, the grave. In Act 1 Falstaff told the Chief Justice that he was born with a white head. Auden wrote that Falstaff’s is a world of play, with no time and no suffering, and that in Henry IV something pulls him out of it into history, where people suffer and die. Music, he wrote, helps Falstaff keep up his illusion: while it plays in Act 2 time stops for him and he does not age. When Falstaff and the Prince next meet, the King’s first words to him are I know thee not, old man.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and Falstaff’s [answer about his age](#/read/henry-iv-2/a1s2:120) in Act 1. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 184, 191, 197–98 and 510–11. Alexander Schmidt’s *Shakespeare-Lexicon* under each word explained. For the notes: the Archbishop in [Act 1, Scene 3](#/read/henry-iv-2/a1s3:37), the Prince’s [good night](#/read/henry-iv-2/a2s4:297) in Act 2, and the Quarto and Folio in the Internet Shakespeare Editions transcriptions.

lenses.label: Balance
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.why: The King’s line has the build of Falstaff’s wish in the first passage, and his speech holds both halves: the slender waist as an order, the means later as an allowance; Auden wrote that no allowance can mend Falstaff’s heart.
lenses.caption: The line sets less against more and body against grace, in two phrases of one build. Rhetoric calls this antithesis. In the first passage Falstaff made a wish of the same build: greater means and a slenderer waist. The waist comes here, as an order. The means come fifteen lines later, in the same word, as an allowance to live on. Where Falstaff said means the King here says grace, which the lexicon reads in this line as virtue. No allowance, Auden wrote, can mend what the rejection does to Falstaff’s heart: what he wants is the Prince’s company.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and antithesis as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. Falstaff’s wish in the first passage, and the allowance later in [the King’s speech](#/read/henry-iv-2/a5s5:57). Alexander Schmidt’s *Shakespeare-Lexicon* under Grace, which quotes this line, and under Mean and Competence. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 190.

auden.says: Donald Pearce took the 1941 class and wrote notes after each lecture. His notes have Auden begin on *Henry IV* by calling Falstaff a comic Iago. Both are detached from the moral side of human dealings and manipulate people: Iago coldly, Falstaff by making a play or game of everything. The play’s true Machiavel, or schemer, he said, is the Prince, who studies Falstaff as his pupil and, at the end of Part 2, drops his old companions without regret, because they are of no more use to him. His father, Auden added, treated the Percies the same way. Auden’s later essay, “The Prince’s Dog,” reads Falstaff differently.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 144–45

auden.says: Later in the same lecture, as Pearce recorded it, Auden called Falstaff an opportunist without conscience and, in private, a man whose hopes have failed him, who wraps himself in fat and plays the child so as not to be hurt. He read Falstaff as a figure for the body of a lazy, swollen, greedy and sick England. He called the old King an able opportunist, and hollow, and said that when the King begs his son for feeling he gets only empty rhetoric back. Falstaff, he said, sees the Prince as his child, and cannot survive in a world that runs on calculation.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 146–48

auden.says: In *The Dyer’s Hand* Auden wrote that the Prince has never deceived himself about Falstaff and rejects him when the rejection will have the greatest political effect. The allowance, which wins the King the admiration of those near him, does not win an audience that knows Falstaff. Falstaff is wholly devoted to the Prince, as to a son of his own, thinks the Prince loves him back, and so is happy in a false belief.
auden.quote: It is Hal’s company he wants, not a pension from the Civil List.
auden.source: “The Prince’s Dog,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 190–91

auden.says: Auden gave a short fable for the three plays with the Falstaff scenes cut. England is infected by its own family doctor. A capable man with no right to practice throws him out, and the patient grows worse, until that man’s son, whom everyone thought a sick man past help, works the cure. Auden listed five things the ideal ruler needs: to know justice from injustice, to be just, to have the strength to enforce justice, to win loyalty, and to be the lawful ruler. Of Henry IV he wrote that no one, the rebels included, names an unjust act of his reign: his injustice was deposing the lawful king.
auden.source: “The Prince’s Dog,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 186–88

auden.says: Of Falstaff’s fatness Auden wrote that a fat man looks half like a small child and half like a woman with child, and that fatness in a man expresses a wish to be mother and child in one, and so to need no one. Falstaff’s great belly and red face, he wrote, bring to mind that England’s body politic is unwell too. He set beside them the play’s lines on a country sick, surfeited and full of rank diseases, the last of them spoken by the King a few lines after the speech in the second passage.
auden.source: “The Prince’s Dog,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 195–98

auden.says: Read as a parable, Auden wrote, Falstaff’s idling and drinking mark the unworldly man, and the Prince is the worldly man at his best. Such a man will treat persons as things when his end requires it, and, seen from outside, the Prince and Iago do the same two things: they deceive and they destroy. Falstaff does nothing and talks without end, so that an audience sees energy and not idleness. Up to the rejection he gives off happiness as the Prince gives off power.
auden.source: “The Prince’s Dog,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 204–06

auden.says: In “Music in Shakespeare” Auden wrote that music, like the sack Falstaff drinks, helps him keep up the illusion of a childlike Eden in which nothing grave can occur, and that above all he deceives himself that the Prince returns his love in full. Shakespeare saves background music for the tavern scene of Act 2. When Peto breaks in, the Prince feels ashamed and Falstaff only disappointed. That moment, Auden wrote, is the turning point of the Prince’s life, and the friendship ends with his good night.
auden.source: “Music in Shakespeare,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 510–11

auden.says: Auden lectured on the Henry plays again in New York in 1946 and 1947. The lectures survive in students’ notes, put together by a later editor. There he said that Hal and Falstaff are lasting opposites and enemies, and that by the end Falstaff is destroyed in body and Hal morally, with nothing of himself remaining.
auden.source: *Lectures on Shakespeare*, reconstructed and edited by Arthur Kirsch (2000), the lecture on *Henry IV, Parts One and Two*, and *Henry V*, p. 110

W. H. Auden, *The Dyer’s Hand and Other Essays* (1962): “The Prince’s Dog,” pp. 183–84, 186–91, 195–98 and 203–07; “Brothers & Others,” p. 221; “Music in Shakespeare,” pp. 510–11.

caveats: What Auden said in class in 1941 is known from notes that a student, Donald Pearce, wrote down after each lecture. It is not Auden’s own text. The opening of the lecture on *Henry IV* (Pearce, pp. 144–45) was read only in snippets of a scanned copy.

Auden’s New York lectures of 1946 and 1947 are an editor’s text made from students’ notes. The book was read here only in snippets of a scanned copy; its page numbers were worked out from a running head and an editor’s note seen in those snippets.

The stresses marked are one reader’s hearing of the lines. The two long lines of the King’s speech and several lines of the third passage could fairly be marked otherwise; *prayers* and *being* are counted as one syllable each and can be heard as two.

The counts of verse and prose follow the text printed here: its lines, its five scenes in Act 4, and its choice of which short speeches to set as verse. Another edition will give slightly different totals.

The second passage leaves out lines 6 to 22 of the King’s speech; lines 9 and 10, left out, also rhyme. Where the text printed here has *slenderer*, *sea-boy* and *give thy repose*, as the Folio of 1623 has, the Quarto of 1600 has *slender*, *season* and *give them repose*.
